rationale: The chapter opens in the third person -- “Doesn’t wisdom cry out” (web:Prov.8.1; Hebrew הֲלֹֽא חָכְמָ֥ה תִקְרָ֑א וּ֝תְבוּנָ֗ה תִּתֵּ֥ן קוֹלָֽהּ, oshb:Prov.8.1) -- describing wisdom crying out at the gates before her own first-person call begins at web:Prov.8.4, “I call to you men” (web:Prov.8.4). The shift from that third-person description to wisdom's own voice at אֲלֵיכֶ֣ם, “to you” (oshb:Prov.8.4), is the content of the very cry the narrator has just introduced in 8.1-3, so the setup and the call proper form one speech-event rather than two. The call moves from the appeal to hear (8.4-11, closing “wisdom is better than rubies” at web:Prov.8.11) into wisdom's self-commendation of her gifts, opened by the declaration אֲֽנִי חָ֭כְמָה (“I, wisdom,” oshb:Prov.8.12), continuing the same first-person voice opened at 8.4 rather than opening a fresh address, and the span runs to the petuchah at oshb:Prov.8.21 (petuchah, single-witness), where “I fill their treasuries” (web:Prov.8.21) closes the gift-commendation just before the cosmological turn of Prov.8.22.
rejected_alternative: Separating the self-declaration at Prov.8.12 from the preceding call to hear (8.1-11) was considered, but the declaration אֲֽנִי חָ֭כְמָה (oshb:Prov.8.12) continues the same first-person voice wisdom opened at 8.4 straight through to the petuchah at Prov.8.21, staying in that voice rather than returning to third-person narration or reopening with a fresh address formula.

device_notes: 8.1-3 narrates wisdom's public cry before the first-person call of 8.4 begins; 8.4-11 and 8.12-21 both run mainly as synthetic parallelism building toward a climactic line (wisdom is better than rubies at 8.11; I fill their treasuries at 8.21) rather than antithetic contrast -- a hymn-like register distinct from the couplet-by-couplet sentences of chs.10-29.

rationale: Direct address returns with “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me” (web:Prov.8.32; Hebrew וְעַתָּ֣ה בָ֭נִים שִׁמְעוּ לִ֑י, oshb:Prov.8.32), a four-word summons attested at three sites book-wide (sweep: 3 verses, skeleton tier -- oshb:Prov.5.7, oshb:Prov.7.24, oshb:Prov.8.32) as a recurring lecture-transition formula rather than wording unique to this seam. What marks 8.32 as this poem's own closing frame is not the wording itself but what follows it: the summons opens directly on the petuchah at oshb:Prov.8.31 (petuchah, single-witness) that ended the cosmological account, and the beatitude form of 8.32-34 gives way to the antithesis closing the chapter: “whoever finds me finds life” (web:Prov.8.35; a ketiv/qere note attaches to oshb:Prov.8.35, single-witness) against “those who hate me love death” (web:Prov.8.36), set life against death in the span's own final couplet at the petuchah in oshb:Prov.8.36 (petuchah, single-witness), which also closes the chapter.
rejected_alternative: Keeping Prov.8.32-36 attached to the cosmological account that precedes it was considered, but the petuchah at Prov.8.31 opens directly onto the beatitude-then-antithesis movement closing the chapter, which the four-word summons -- a recurring lecture-transition formula -- introduces rather than distinguishes.

device_notes: 8.32-34 pairs beatitude form with imperative address (hear instruction, and be wise; watching daily at my gates, waiting at my door posts), and 8.35-36 closes with antithetic parallelism (whoever finds me finds life / he who sins against me wrongs his own soul), setting life against death in the chapter's final couplet -- the poem's own inclusio answer to the beatitude that opened the call at 8.32-34.
